## 1. What you'll build, and why

This is the last hop, and the payoff. You'll write **IRGen** — lower the SIL module to **LLVM IR** —
and `clang` turns that into a native executable. For the first time since Phase 1, programs **run**:
`if`/`while`/`for`, functions, recursion all execute, and `swiftml2`'s output matches `swiftc`
byte-for-byte. That's **Milestone M2**, and the end of Phase 2.

- **You implement:** the SIL-instruction and terminator lowering in `irgen.ml` (`gen_instr`,
  `gen_term`). Everything upstream (front-end, SIL, SILGen) is given and complete.
- **Outcome:** `swiftml2 build foo.swift -o foo && ./foo` produces the same output as `swiftc`.

Here is a complete example to keep in view while you fill the skeleton. It has one function with
parameters of two different types, then calls that function from the top level:

```swift
func choose(_ value: Int, _ addOne: Bool) -> Int {
  if addOne {
    return value + 1
  }
  return value
}

print(choose(41, true))
```

`swiftml2 --emit-llvm` produces this unoptimized LLVM module:

```llvm
; swiftml Phase-2 LLVM IR
declare i32 @printf(ptr, ...)
@.fmt_int = private unnamed_addr constant [6 x i8] c"%lld\0A\00"
@.fmt_str = private unnamed_addr constant [4 x i8] c"%s\0A\00"
@.fmt_dbl = private unnamed_addr constant [4 x i8] c"%g\0A\00"
@.btrue  = private unnamed_addr constant [5 x i8] c"true\00"
@.bfalse = private unnamed_addr constant [6 x i8] c"false\00"

define i64 @choose(i64 %arg0, i1 %arg1) {
bb0:
  %t0 = alloca i64
  %t1 = alloca i1
  store i64 %arg0, ptr %t0
  store i1 %arg1, ptr %t1
  %t2 = load i1, ptr %t1
  br i1 %t2, label %bb1, label %bb2
bb1:
  %t3 = load i64, ptr %t0
  %t4 = add i64 %t3, 1
  ret i64 %t4
bb2:
  %t5 = load i64, ptr %t0
  ret i64 %t5
}

define i32 @main() {
bb0:
  %t0 = call i64 @choose(i64 41, i1 1)
  call i32 (ptr, ...) @printf(ptr @.fmt_int, i64 %t0)
  ret i32 0
}

```

The declarations and format strings are given scaffolding. `Int` becomes `i64`, while `Bool`
becomes `i1`, a one-bit integer. `@choose` receives `%arg0` and `%arg1`, stores them in the stack
slots used by raw SIL, and branches on the loaded `Bool`. Each branch returns an `i64`.

In `@main`, the literals `41` and `true` appear directly as the operands `41` and `1`. The call
produces `%t0`, which the `printf` call consumes. Temporary numbering restarts in each function,
which is why both functions can have a `%t0`. The final `ret i32 0` reports successful process
termination. Compiling and running the module prints `42`.

## 2. Concepts in depth

### The easy hop — because SIL did the hard work

IRGen is the shortest pass in the compiler, and that's the point: **SILGen already built the
control-flow graph, so IRGen is almost a one-to-one transliteration.** SIL is raw and memory-based;
LLVM IR is also memory-capable (it has `alloca`/`load`/`store`) and block-structured.

This concept adds no Swift syntax — the grammar is still concept 07's. What it adds is the mapping
between two IRs, so this table is the specification of your work: every SIL form concept 08 can
emit, and the LLVM line it becomes. `<-- yours` marks the cases behind the two `TODO(09)` holes;
the rest is given.

**Instructions** (`gen_instr`). Several emit *no line at all* into the function body — they only
bind the SIL value to an operand, which is a shape worth expecting before you meet it:

In the table, `$T` stands for a SIL type. `<ty>`, `<ty-a>`, `<ty-b>`, and `<ret>` stand for the
corresponding LLVM type spellings produced by `llvm_type`, such as `i64`, `i1`, `double`, or `void`.

| SIL | LLVM |
|---|---|
| `%n = integer_literal $Int, 7` | the operand `7` — no line (given, as the pattern) |
| `%n = integer_literal $Bool, true` | the operand `1` — no line (given) |
| `%n = float_literal $Double, 1.5` | a hex float operand — no line (given) |
| `%n = string_literal $String, "hi"` | a `private unnamed_addr constant` global (given) |
| `%n = alloc_stack $T  // x` | `%tK = alloca <ty>`, hoisted to the entry block (given) |
| `%n = load %a $T` | `%tK = load <ty>, ptr %a` `<-- yours` |
| `store %v to %a` | `store <ty> %v, ptr %a` — no result `<-- yours` |
| `%n = binop "+" %a, %b $Int` | `%tK = add i64 %a, %b` (the given `gen_binop` table) `<-- yours` |
| `%n = unop "-" %a $T` | `%tK = sub i64 0, %a` for `Int`; `%tK = fneg double %a` for `Double` `<-- yours` |
| `%n = function_ref @f` | the operand `@f` — no line `<-- yours` |
| `%n = apply %f(%a, %b)` | `%tK = call <ret> %f(<ty-a> %a, <ty-b> %b)`, or `call void …` with no result `<-- yours` |
| `%n = apply @print(%a)` | a `printf` call (the given `gen_print`) `<-- yours` |

**Terminators** (`gen_term`) — the CFG, and the one asymmetry in the whole pass:

| SIL | LLVM |
|---|---|
| `br bbN` | `br label %bbN` `<-- yours` |
| `cond_br %c, bbT, bbF` | `br i1 %c, label %bbT, label %bbF` `<-- yours` |
| `return %v` | `ret <the function's return type> %v` `<-- yours` |
| `return` | `ret void` — **but `ret i32 0` in `@main`** `<-- yours` |
| `unreachable` | `unreachable` — a real LLVM instruction `<-- yours` |

The asymmetry is `@main`. In SIL it is an ordinary function returning `$()`; in LLVM it is the C
entry point, whose `i32` result *is* the process's exit code, so a valueless `return` there has to
become `ret i32 0`. Blocks and their labels carry across unchanged, which is why an `--emit-llvm`
dump closely follows the structure of the `--emit-sil` dump for the same program, even though the
instructions use LLVM syntax.

One LLVM rule is worth learning right now: **every `alloca` goes at the top of the entry block**
(the given `gen_allocas` does this for you). An `alloca` reserves stack space that is only returned
when the *function exits* — not at the end of a scope — so an `alloca` emitted inside a loop body
would grow the stack on every iteration until it overflowed. Hoisting them all to the entry block
makes the stack frame fixed-size. It cannot create a name collision: SILGen gives every value in a
function a unique `%n`, so every allocation has a distinct key in `operands`. `gen_allocas` assigns
those allocations LLVM names using `fresh_temp`; ordinary instruction lowering uses the same
counter afterward, so it cannot reuse any of their `%tN` names. Entry-block allocation is also what
LLVM's own `mem2reg` pass requires before it will promote a slot to a register. (Concept 20's
benchmark shows exactly how this bites at a few million iterations.)

The control-flow work — turning a tree into a graph and threading `break`/`continue` to the right
blocks — happened in SILGen. IRGen walks that finished graph and translates it to LLVM. This
separation is one reason for having SIL. SIL also gives later compiler passes a stable, Swift-aware
representation to verify, analyze, and optimize before lowering it to a backend.

### The one real job: a value map, and *types*

IRGen maintains one table. It maps each **SIL value `%n` to an LLVM operand**. A constant maps to
itself (`Int_lit 5` becomes the operand `5`); a `string_literal` maps to a global; every other
instruction emits an LLVM line and maps the SIL value to a fresh `%tK`. The subtle part is
**types**. LLVM is strongly typed, so an `add` on `Int` is `add i64` but on `Double` is
`fadd double`, and a comparison is `icmp slt i64`
(integers) vs `fcmp olt double` (floats) — producing an `i1` (LLVM's Bool). Floating-point `!=`
uses `fcmp une`: "unordered or not equal" keeps `NaN != NaN` true, as Swift requires. The SIL
function's `val_ty` map gives you each value's type; the given `gen_binop` table picks the right
opcode.

`print` lowers to a `printf` call keyed on the argument's type: `%lld` for `Int`, a `select` between
`"true"`/`"false"` globals for `Bool`, `%s` for a `String`. And `@main` returns `i32` (the C entry
point: `return` → `ret i32 0`), while other functions return their declared LLVM type.

![The complete Phase-2 pipeline: source → tokens → AST → typed AST → SIL → LLVM IR → native. IRGen (concept 09) is the last hop; then `clang` links it and the program runs.](figs/pipeline.png)

### Running checks what structure alone cannot

Concept 08 could *emit* SIL but not run it. Concept 09 adds Phase 2's end-to-end semantic check.
Consider a plausible IRGen mistake: lowering SIL `sub %a, %b` as LLVM `sub i64 %b, %a`. The LLVM is
well formed, and a structural test that only looks for `sub i64` passes, but `print(9 - 4)` prints
`-5` instead of `5`. Building and running the program exposes the reversed operands.

This is the lesson behind the whole project's testing strategy: structural checks catch mistakes in
the IR's shape, while **behavioral parity against `swiftc`** catches well-formed IR with the wrong
meaning. That is why the cram tests here inspect the LLVM and also **build and run the programs**.

### Handing off to LLVM (and what we're not doing yet)

We emit *unoptimized* LLVM IR and let `clang` assemble and link it. `clang` runs LLVM's own optimizer
and backend — so even our naive, load/store-heavy IR comes out as decent native code. swiftc does the
same handoff, but only after its **own** SIL optimizer runs first (that's Phase 4 for us). Two things
we deliberately scope out, all documented:

- **`Double` printing** isn't matched to swiftc. Swift prints just enough decimal digits to
  preserve the exact `Double` value when the text is parsed again; C's `%g` does not.
  **`String`** concatenation and comparison need a runtime we haven't built. The parity corpus
  therefore covers `Int`, `Bool`, control flow, functions, and `Double` computations whose result
  is observed through a `Bool`.
- **Definite initialization** — Swift's mandatory "variable used before being initialized" pass on
  the SIL CFG — is *vacuous* for us, because every `let`/`var` is initialized at its declaration.
  Adding uninitialized `var x: Int` and a DI dataflow pass (Exercise 1) is the genuine version, and a
  direct sequel to the "missing return" analysis from concept 07.

> Oracle: `swift/lib/IRGen/IRGenSIL.cpp` is `visitSILInstruction` for each SIL opcode — the analogue
> of your `gen_instr`. swiftc's IRGen is far larger because it also lowers ARC, generics, and value
> witnesses; ours handles the Phase-2 subset.

### The diagnostics you emit

**None, again.** IRGen runs on SIL that sema accepted and the verifier passed, so there is nothing
left for it to refuse: every wording the tests compare belongs to concepts 05–07, and `--emit-llvm`
and `build` run the whole front end first and bail on its errors before IRGen is reached.

Two failures are still possible, and neither is a Swift diagnostic. Ill-typed LLVM — an `add i64` on
an `i1`, a `ret void` where the signature says `i64` — is caught by **clang**, which prints its own
error and makes `build` fail; treat that as a bug in your mapping table, and note that it is a real
check the cram files lean on (`irgen-terms.t` ends by building the program, not just printing it).
Second, the exit code: `@main`'s `ret i32 0` is the *process's* exit status, so a program that
prints nothing must still exit 0 — `run-arith.t` pins that, because it is the kind of thing that
only shows up when something later depends on it.

## 3. Build it, step by step

One skeleton, `irgen.ml`, and two holes in it — `gen_instr` and `gen_term`, both inside `gen_func`.
The plumbing is given: `llvm_type`, the output buffers, `fresh_temp ()`, the `operands` value map,
`gen_binop`'s opcode table, `gen_print`, `gen_allocas`, and the loop over blocks.
`lookup_operand value` reads a value's LLVM operand, while `bind_operand value llvm_operand` records
one. The literal cases of `gen_instr` are given too, as the pattern to copy: they bind an operand and
emit nothing.

The normal `--emit-llvm` path needs both holes because every function ends in a terminator. The lab
also has a test-only `--emit-llvm-instrs` mode. It omits block terminators, producing deliberately
incomplete IR that is useful only for inspecting `gen_instr`. This lets its cases turn green before
you start `gen_term`. Keep the final catch-all `failwith` while adding instruction cases above it;
the OCaml file must still type-check before any test can run.

1. **`gen_instr`**, working down the instruction table in §2. Emit a line with `emit "…"`; when the
   instruction has a result, give it a `fresh_temp ()` and record it with `bind_operand` so later
   instructions can name it. Types come from `llvm_type (value_type value)`. Not every SIL
   instruction both emits an LLVM line and produces a result. Literals and `function_ref` only bind
   an operand; they emit no line. A `store` emits a line but binds nothing. A non-void call emits
   `%tK = call …` and records `%tK`, while a void call emits `call void …` without recording
   a result.
2. **`gen_term`**, the five terminator forms. `is_main` is in scope for the `@main` exception.

Then `./lab.exe build p.swift -o p && ./p` on anything from §4 — clang will tell you at once if the
IR is not well-typed.

Reference: `solution/irgen.ml`.

## 4. Test it

```bash
make lab C=phase2-types-flow/09-sil-to-llvm
```

Five cram files (`make lab C=… T=run-control` runs one), a unit suite grouped by hole, and the
oracle. The first two read the IR; the rest **build the program and run it**, which is the point of
this concept:

- `irgen-instrs.t` — test-only `--emit-llvm-instrs` down the instruction table: literals as
  operands,
  `alloca`/`load`/`store` model, the entry-block alloca rule (a `let` inside a loop still allocas
  in `bb0`), the typed arithmetic mnemonics, the signed `icmp` predicates, `sub i64 0, x` for
  unary minus, `function_ref` + `apply` becoming one `call`, and `print`'s two shapes.
- `irgen-terms.t` — the five terminators, `@main`'s `ret i32 0`, an `unreachable` that survives
  into LLVM, and a `build` at the end, because printable is not the same as well-typed.
- `run-arith.t` — compiled and run: integer arithmetic and Swift's truncating division and
  signed remainder, unary minus, Double comparisons including NaN, `Bool` printing,
  `&&`/`||` **short-circuiting** (a program that
  would print if the right operand were evaluated), and a silent program's exit code.
- `run-control.t` — `if`/`else if`, `while`, `for` (including an empty range), `break` out of a
  loop with a bound of 100, `continue` in a `for` — the case that caught the real bug — and
  nested loops where each of `break` and `continue` addresses the inner one only.
- `run-funcs.t` — argument order, mixed argument types, and nested calls, recursion (`fib 20`),
  mutual recursion,
  `Void` returns and an early bare `return`, a loop inside a function, and `gcd`/`collatz` as a
  smoke test for the whole phase.
- `test_irgen.ml` (alcotest `irgen`) — the same in-process, one group per hole plus a "given"
  group that counts allocas and checks they are all in the entry block. Reading the text lets a
  case ask *where* a line landed, which the cram greps cannot.
- `oracle.t` — **the headline, and Milestone M2**: 29 programs from `oracle-corpus.txt` are
  compiled by `swiftc -Onone` and by `./lab.exe build`, both binaries are run, and stdout and
  exit code must be identical. The numbers in the other files were written down once; this one
  asks swiftc on every run.
- `test_exercises.ml` (Alcotest `exercises-09`) — the three optional §6 exercises. It compiles
  and runs focused programs out of process, so parser and generated-code hangs time out.

The `gen_instr` cases can pass before `gen_term` is started. The terminator and execution files stay
red until the emitted module is complete. A failing case shows the wanted and printed output side by
side.

Every generated executable runs through a five-second test deadline. A mistaken back-edge therefore
fails with exit `124` instead of leaving `make lab` stuck in an infinite loop.

The terminator tests use `--emit-llvm-terms <kind>` to select `br`, `cond-br`, `return-value`,
`return-none`, or `unreachable`. An unfinished terminator form therefore cannot hide the result of
a completed one.

While working on the first hole, run only its focused file:

```bash
make lab C=phase2-types-flow/09-sil-to-llvm T=irgen-instrs
```

## 5. Benchmark it

The benchmark runs this Collatz workload for every starting value below 500,000:

```swift
var total = 0
for start in 1 ..< 500000 {
  var n = start
  while n != 1 {
    if n % 2 == 0 {
      n = n / 2
    } else {
      n = 3 * n + 1
    }
    total = total + 1
  }
}
print(total)
```

Run it from `course/` after completing both holes:

```console
$ make bench C=phase2-types-flow/09-sil-to-llvm
IRGen runtime benchmark -- Collatz for starts 1..<500000
  output: 62134644 (all five binaries agree)
  native runtime, best of 5 after one warm-up:
    swiftml (clang default)  0.209 s
    swiftml + clang -O2      0.045 s
    swiftc -Onone            0.670 s
    swiftc -O                0.070 s
    swiftc -Ounchecked       0.046 s
  clang -O2 speedup: 4.69x
  swiftc -O speedup: 9.61x
  unchecked gap: 1.02x (swiftc / swiftml)
```

These are measured reference-solution results; timings vary by machine. The runner first requires
byte-identical output from all five binaries, then reports the best of five executions after one
warm-up. It has no speed gate because this concept deliberately emits unoptimized code.

The flags select the optimization level. With no flag, clang uses `-O0`: it preserves the raw
`alloca`, `load`, and `store` heavy shape closely. `clang -O2` enables LLVM's standard optimizations
for speed. `swiftc -Onone` compiles without optimization, while `swiftc -O` compiles with
optimizations for speed. `swiftc -Ounchecked` also optimizes, but removes runtime safety checks such
as integer-overflow checks.

The `clang -O2` row is useful: without changing our SIL, LLVM removes much of the raw memory traffic
and makes the program about 4.65 times faster. For this small scalar subset, we could defer much of
the optimization work to LLVM. That shows IRGen already produces optimization-friendly LLVM IR.

It does not make a SIL optimizer redundant. Swift-specific passes can reason about ownership,
dynamic dispatch, and generics before those ideas disappear into lower-level IR. Optimized SIL can
also feed a backend that does not use LLVM. Phase 4 builds that target-independent layer, starting
with **mem2reg**, then constant folding, CSE, and inlining.

The `-Ounchecked` result makes the comparison clearer. Once swiftc removes its safety checks, its
`0.046 s` is effectively the same as our `0.045 s`. For this non-overflowing scalar workload, both
pipelines therefore hand LLVM code it can optimize to the same performance class.

That result does not establish general performance parity. `-Ounchecked` changes Swift's safety
semantics, and our subset omits most of Swift's language and runtime. The benchmark isolates one
small program and one major source of overhead.

With richer Swift constructs, SIL optimization can produce faster code than a basic translation
straight to LLVM. Reference counting, protocol and class dispatch, generic calls, closure captures,
and `Array` checks still have explicit Swift meaning in SIL. SIL passes can remove redundant
retain/release operations, replace dynamic dispatch with direct calls, specialize generic code, and
eliminate or move collection checks out of loops. A basic lowering turns many of these operations
into pointer loads, stores, and opaque runtime calls; LLVM can no longer recover all the Swift
semantics needed to prove the same transformations. LLVM then optimizes the lower-level result, so
the SIL and LLVM optimizers complement each other. This division is described in
`swift/docs/OptimizerDesign.md` and `swift/docs/HighLevelSILOptimizations.rst`.

## 6. Exercises

These are optional. `make exercises C=phase2-types-flow/09-sil-to-llvm` runs only their
self-detecting suite. They also appear in `make lab` as `TODO (optional)` until you start one.

1. **Definite initialization.** Add uninitialized `var x: Int` (a `var` with a type annotation and no
   initializer): parser, an `Ast` node, sema binds it, SILGen `alloc_stack`s but does not `store`.
   Then write a **forward dataflow pass on the SIL CFG**: a slot is "initialized on entry to a block"
   iff it's initialized on exit of *all* predecessors; a `load` from an uninitialized slot is
   "variable '…' used before being initialized." Match `swiftc`.
2. **`Double` output parity.** Print just enough decimal digits to preserve the exact `Double`
   value when the text is parsed again. Use the Ryū or Grisu algorithm, or shell out, and make
   `print(0.1 + 0.2)` match `swiftc`.
3. **A tiny runtime.** Add a `runtime.c` (compiled and linked by the driver) with `swiftml_print_int`
   etc., instead of inlining `printf` calls — the seed of a real standard library (Phase 7).

## 7. Recap & what's next — **Milestone M2**

Phase 2 is complete. In 05–07, you extended every front-end layer — the lexer, parser, AST, and Sema
— to support types, control flow, and functions. This included bidirectional type checking and the
semantic rules that make those constructs sound. SILGen then added the **SIL** middle (08), and
**IRGen** now lowers SIL to LLVM and runs the result (09). The core pipeline follows swiftc's:
`Parse → Sema → SILGen → SIL → IRGen → LLVM → native`. On the
`Int`/`Bool`/control-flow/functions corpus, the output matches `swiftc` byte-for-byte (`Double`
printing and `String` are the documented gaps of §2).

Two directions open up. **Phase 3** grows the *language* — `struct`, `enum` (ADTs), pattern matching,
`Optional` — the value types Swift is built from. **Phase 4** grows the *compiler* — the SIL
**optimizer**, starting with **mem2reg**, where the raw, load/store-heavy SIL you've been emitting is
promoted to **SSA** and you learn SSA properly, by watching it happen. That's the deliberate payoff of
choosing memory-based SIL back in concept 08.

## 8. Appendix — full solution

Mirrors `solution/irgen.ml`. The shape: a constant maps a SIL value to an LLVM operand; an instruction
emits a line and maps its result to a fresh `%tK`; types come from the function's `val_ty`.

```ocaml
let gen_instr (value, instruction) =
  match (instruction : Sil.instr) with
  | Sil.Int_lit integer -> bind_operand value (string_of_int integer)
  | Sil.Bool_lit boolean -> bind_operand value (if boolean then "1" else "0")
  | Sil.Float_lit number ->
      bind_operand value (Printf.sprintf "0x%016LX" (Int64.bits_of_float number))
  | Sil.String_lit text -> bind_operand value (add_string_const text)
  (* emitted in the entry block by the given gen_allocas — see §2 *)
  | Sil.Alloc_stack _ -> ()
  | Sil.Load address ->
      let result_operand = fresh_temp () in
      emit (Printf.sprintf "  %s = load %s, ptr %s\n" result_operand
              (llvm_type (value_type value)) (lookup_operand address));
      bind_operand value result_operand
  | Sil.Store (stored_value, address) ->
      emit (Printf.sprintf "  store %s %s, ptr %s\n"
              (llvm_type (value_type stored_value)) (lookup_operand stored_value)
              (lookup_operand address))
  | Sil.Binop (operator, left, right) -> gen_binop value operator left right
  | Sil.Unop (Ast.Neg, operand) ->
      let result_operand = fresh_temp () in
      (if value_type operand = Types.TDouble then
         emit (Printf.sprintf "  %s = fneg double %s\n" result_operand (lookup_operand operand))
       else emit (Printf.sprintf "  %s = sub i64 0, %s\n" result_operand (lookup_operand operand)));
      bind_operand value result_operand
  | Sil.Func_ref name -> bind_operand value ("@" ^ name)
  | Sil.Apply (function_operand, arguments) ->
      let argument_list =
        String.concat ", "
          (List.map (fun argument ->
             Printf.sprintf "%s %s" (llvm_type (value_type argument))
               (lookup_operand argument)) arguments)
      in
      let return_type = value_type value in
      if return_type = Types.TVoid then
        emit (Printf.sprintf "  call void %s(%s)\n"
                (lookup_operand function_operand) argument_list)
      else (
        let result_operand = fresh_temp () in
        emit (Printf.sprintf "  %s = call %s %s(%s)\n" result_operand
                (llvm_type return_type) (lookup_operand function_operand) argument_list);
        bind_operand value result_operand)
  | Sil.Print printed_value -> gen_print printed_value

let gen_term (terminator : Sil.term) =
  match terminator with
  | Sil.Br target -> emit (Printf.sprintf "  br label %%bb%d\n" target)
  | Sil.Cond_br (condition, then_block, else_block) ->
      emit (Printf.sprintf "  br i1 %s, label %%bb%d, label %%bb%d\n"
              (lookup_operand condition) then_block else_block)
  | Sil.Return None -> emit (if is_main then "  ret i32 0\n" else "  ret void\n")
  | Sil.Return (Some return_value) ->
      emit (Printf.sprintf "  ret %s %s\n"
              (llvm_type function_definition.Sil.ret) (lookup_operand return_value))
  | Sil.Unreachable -> emit "  unreachable\n"
```

## 9. Exercise solutions

### 1 — definite initialization (a SIL dataflow pass)

With `var x: Int` lowering to an `alloc_stack` and no `store`, run a forward dataflow over the SIL
CFG. For each block compute `in[b] = ⋂ out[p]` over predecessors `p` (the entry's `in` is the empty
set; a parameter slot starts initialized); walk the block updating the set on each `Store`, and on a
`Load` of a slot **not** in the set, report "variable '…' used before being initialized." Iterate to a
fixed point (a worklist). This is the same forward-meet-over-paths shape you'll reuse for liveness and
reaching-definitions in Phase 4 — DI is the gentlest instance, and it's *mandatory* in swiftc because
it's a soundness guarantee, not an optimization.

### 2 — Double output parity

`print(d)` currently emits `printf("%g\n", d)`, which rounds to 6 significant figures. Swift prints
the *shortest* decimal string that round-trips back to the same `Double`. Implement Ryū (or Grisu),
or call into a C helper; format the result and pad/trim to Swift's rules (e.g. `1.0` prints as `1.0`,
`0.1` as `0.1`). This is a self-contained, surprisingly deep numerics exercise.

### 3 — a runtime.c

Have the driver also compile a small `runtime.c` (declaring `void swiftml_print_int(long long)` etc.)
and link it in, and make IRGen `call @swiftml_print_int` instead of inlining `printf`. Now the
print/format logic lives in C you control — the first brick of a standard library, which Phase 7
turns into `Array`/`String`/`Dictionary`.
```
